story.title: Widespread Student Protests Lead to School Closures Across France
story.summary: Protests by French high school students over school conditions have escalated, resulting in the closure of around 400 schools and over 200 injuries. Students have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Toulouse, and Lille, demanding better resources. The unrest has prompted warnings from officials about the safety of students amidst the violence.

timeline_highlights.title: Protests Erupt in Spain as Parliament Rejects Housing Crisis Measures
timeline_highlights.summary: Protests erupted across Spain ahead of a parliamentary vote on housing measures, following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman that sparked public outrage. Hundreds demonstrated in Madrid and other cities, expressing their discontent with the government's handling of the housing crisis. The proposed measures were ultimately rejected by opposition lawmakers, intensifying pressure on the government and raising speculation about a potential snap election.

explore_lenses.label: What are students demanding beyond closures?
explore_lenses.title: Resource shortages are at the center
explore_lenses.summary: The protests began around school conditions rather than a single national policy. Student representatives describe staffing, facilities and workload problems, while the government has acknowledged the original grievances as legitimate even as it condemns violence.

claims.text: Students and their organizations cite unreplaced teachers, deteriorating buildings, overcrowded or demanding schedules, and pressure linked to the Parcoursup admissions system among their complaints.
Ryad Rani, president of the Union syndicale lycéenne, called for large-scale teacher recruitment and an emergency plan for school buildings.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said the initial high-school movement was legitimate, but said it had been overtaken by violent fringe groups.

explore_lenses.label: Why have safety measures become so sweeping?
explore_lenses.title: Officials cite injuries, damage and mixed crowds
explore_lenses.summary: The scale of school disruptions reflects safety decisions as well as protest participation. Authorities have responded with closures, remote learning and local protest restrictions, while students have accused police of excessive force.

claims.text: On October 2, the Education Ministry counted 564 high schools that had faced action or disruption during the day; more than 400 were closed, out of about 3,700 high schools nationally.
Officials said closures were tied in part to damaged fire-protection systems and threats or attacks against staff; some schools were to provide classes remotely.

The Interior Ministry said 1,949 people were arrested on October 1 in connection with the blockades; it reported 305 injured police officers and gendarmes that day. Geffray separately reported 65 injured education staff and about 170 injured students since the movement began.
Students interviewed by AFP said tear gas and other police tactics had caused injuries; authorities characterize the response as necessary to address violence and protect people and property.

explore_lenses.label: What could happen after the October 2 protests?
explore_lenses.title: Talks and tighter policing are proceeding together
explore_lenses.summary: The government is combining meetings with student, parent and staff representatives with restrictions near closed schools. That creates two immediate paths: limited de-escalation through concessions and dialogue, or further confrontations if planned mobilizations continue.

claims.text: Geffray scheduled October 2 meetings with education unions, parent associations, student organizations including Renouveau lycéen, Les Lycéens! and the Union syndicale lycéenne, and the National High School Life Council.
The government withdrew a proposed fee for non-scholarship students enrolling in BTS programs or preparatory classes, a step reported as an attempt to ease tensions.

Prefects imposed bans on demonstrations around schools closed on October 2; in Nancy, the prefect authorized drone imaging near the city center and Lycée Jean-Prouvé through 8 p.m., citing risks to public order and safety.
Forecast: Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said he feared possible urban violence later on October 2, over the weekend, or during a further mobilization called for Tuesday, October 6.

story_report.summary: Student protests over conditions in French high schools disrupted 564 schools on October 2, prompting the closure of more than 400 of roughly 3,700 high schools nationwide. The unrest has been accompanied by more than 200 reported injuries, though official counts cover different groups and periods. Students are seeking improved resources, while Education Minister Édouard Geffray said a legitimate initial movement had been overtaken by violent fringe groups.

sections.heading: Students Cite Strained School Conditions
sections.body: Students and their organizations have cited unreplaced teachers, deteriorating buildings, overcrowded or demanding schedules, and pressure associated with the Parcoursup admissions system. Ryad Rani, president of the Union syndicale lycéenne, called for large-scale teacher recruitment and an emergency plan for school buildings. The reporting documents broad shared grievances, but does not establish a single negotiated list of demands accepted by all participants.

sections.heading: Arrests and Injuries Complicate Toll
sections.body: The Interior Ministry said 1,949 people were arrested in connection with the blockades on October 1 and reported 305 injured police officers and gendarmes that day. Geffray separately reported 65 injured education staff and about 170 injured students since the movement began. Students interviewed by AFP said tear gas and other police tactics caused injuries, while authorities described their response as necessary to address violence and protect people and property.

sections.heading: Government Mixes Talks With Restrictions
sections.body: Geffray scheduled meetings on October 2 with education unions, parent groups, student organizations and the National High School Life Council. The government also withdrew a proposed fee for non-scholarship students entering BTS programs or preparatory classes, in a reported effort to ease tensions. Meanwhile, prefects banned demonstrations around closed schools, and Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin warned of possible urban violence later that day, over the weekend or during a further mobilization called for October 6.

unresolved.text: It remains unclear whether the meetings and withdrawal of the proposed fee will satisfy student organizations, or whether the planned October 6 mobilization will proceed at the anticipated scale.
